title: Milo's Cafe: a neighborhood site with a live patio
tag: Café and restaurant website, Morrisville, NC
summaryLead: Milo's Cafe is a European-style all-day café in Morrisville, NC, serving focaccia sandwiches, Lavazza espresso, matcha and crepes. We built a single-page site to answer the three things a hungry visitor wants to know before they leave the house: what is on the menu, are you open, and can we sit outside.
summaryMore: The site is hand-written HTML, CSS and vanilla JavaScript with no framework and no build step. The menu is structured data rather than a PDF, the open-or-closed status is worked out from the café's hours in Eastern time, and an illustrated patio scene reads current conditions for Morrisville from the free Open-Meteo weather service. If that request fails, the page quietly falls back to showing the day's hours.

stack.name: Delivery
stack.detail: One self-contained HTML file with no framework, no build step and no database to maintain.

stack.name: Markup and accessibility
stack.detail: HTML5 landmarks, ARIA tabs for Food and Drinks, live regions, and an accessible name on every control. 'Pair it' results are announced to screen readers.

stack.name: Styling and type
stack.detail: Hand-written CSS with design tokens. Newsreader for headlines and Hanken Grotesk for body text.

stack.name: Menu data
stack.detail: 69 items held as structured data and rendered into tabs, with live search across names and descriptions, a meat-free filter that matches ingredient names, and a star on guest favourites. The page tells guests to ask about allergens.

stack.name: Pair it
stack.detail: Picks a combination from hand-picked food and drink lists based on the guest's mood. If either is left empty it chooses at random.

stack.name: Open or closed
stack.detail: Hours stored as data and checked against the current Eastern time, shown in the top bar.

stack.name: Patio scene
stack.detail: Inline SVG driven by time of day and weather: sun and moon follow the day, the sky blends between dawn, golden hour and dusk, café lights come on after dark, and rain falls when it rains. The verdict comes from feels-like temperature, wind and rain.

stack.name: Weather data
stack.detail: Current conditions for Morrisville from the Open-Meteo forecast API (no key needed), refreshed every 30 seconds. If the request fails, the page falls back to showing the day's hours.

stack.name: Ordering
stack.detail: Order buttons link to the café's SpotOn online ordering page, and a sticky Order and Call bar keeps both actions in reach. There is no cart on the site.

stack.name: Motion
stack.detail: The intro, custom cursor, marquee and count-up are skipped for visitors who ask their device for reduced motion.

chapters.title: A patio you can check before you drive over
chapters.challenge: Outdoor seating is a big part of the draw, but a photo cannot tell a visitor whether today is a patio day. Weather apps do not know where the shade is or whether the café is open.
chapters.solution: An illustrated SVG patio scene driven by the time of day and the weather. The sun and moon follow the day, the sky blends between dawn, golden hour and dusk, café lights come on after dark, and rain falls when it rains. A verdict line is worked out from feels-like temperature, wind and rain, and a slider lets visitors scrub through the whole day.
chapters.outcome: A practical answer to "should we sit outside?" that refreshes itself every 30 seconds, with no extra photography and no manual updates.

chapters.title: A menu that is data, not a PDF
chapters.challenge: Café menus usually live in PDFs or photos that cannot be searched, are hard to read on a phone and are invisible to search engines and screen readers.
chapters.solution: All 69 food and drink items are stored as structured data and rendered into Food and Drinks tabs, with live search across names and descriptions, a meat-free filter and a star on guest favourites. The filter is a guide only, and the page tells guests to ask about ingredients and allergens.
chapters.outcome: Visitors find what they want in seconds on a phone, and adding a seasonal drink or changing a description is a one-line edit.

chapters.title: Helping the undecided order
chapters.challenge: First-time visitors face dozens of items and no obvious place to start, which slows the decision and can push people towards the safest, most familiar choice.
chapters.solution: A small "pair it" tool. Guests pick a mood for food (savory, sweet or light) and for a drink (coffee, matcha, seasonal or not coffee), and it suggests a combination from hand-picked lists. Leave either one empty and it surprises them. Results are announced to screen readers.
chapters.outcome: A low-pressure way into the menu with no account, no tracking and no back end.

results.title: Answers before the question
results.text: Today's hours and the patio verdict sit in the top bar before anyone scrolls, and a sticky Order and Call bar keeps the two main actions in reach.

results.title: A menu people can use
results.text: Real text that can be searched, filtered, read on a phone and picked up by assistive technology and search engines, instead of a PDF.

results.title: Motion that respects people
results.text: The intro, custom cursor, marquee and count-up are all skipped for visitors who ask their device for reduced motion.
